articles.title: I’m part of the team writing the next bible of psychiatry – for the first time, the DSM will use biology to understand mental disorders
articles.author:
<name>Anand Kumar, Professor and Department Head of Psychiatry, University of Illinois Chicago</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/anand-kumar-1404830"/>
paras: The “ bible” of clinical psychiatry – the DSM, short for the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders – is one of the most popular psychiatry reference books around the world. Clinicians use it to diagnose patients and scientists use it to guide research.

Despite its wide impact, the DSM has never integrated biology in its diagnoses of mental illness. This omission was largely because the underlying biology of mental illness was too preliminary to be included in such a widely used clinical manual.

The most recent version of the DSM – the DSM-5 , released in 2013 – has attracted significant criticism from clinicians and researchers , including on how its lack of objective biological measures risks medicalizing human suffering and reducing the validity of psychiatric diagnoses.

The American Psychiatric Association announced that it will release the next edition of the DSM in the coming years, and one of its major plans is to modernize the manual by introducing biology. I was a member of the DSM’s strategic committee between May 2024 and August 2026 and contributed to the subcommittee tasked with integrating neurobiology into the manual.

Researchers’ understanding of the biology of mental disorders is still slowly evolving. So my DSM colleagues and I decided to take a more nuanced approach to incorporate neurobiology into the diagnosis of psychiatric conditions.

Biological factors are mechanisms that may be involved in the development of a disease but have not yet crystallized into something that can be quantifiably measured in the lab. These factors can be physiological, genetic or biochemical.

In contrast, biological markers – called biomarkers for short – are characteristics that can be objectively measured and used to evaluate a biological process, including how well someone is responding to a particular treatment. Biomarkers can be collected through blood tests , imaging scans and other methods that reveal factors associated with a specific disease.

Biomarkers are widely used in medicine. For example, hemoglobin A1C levels are used to diagnose and monitor diabetes, cholesterol levels to determine cardiovascular risk, and CT scans to measure the size of a tumor.

There are currently no scientifically valid biomarkers for any psychiatric condition, with the exception of certain proteins used to diagnose Alzheimer’s disease . The primary reason for this chasm between psychiatry and the rest of medicine is that knowledge about the biological basis of mental disorders lags behind other medical disorders .

The biological changes underlying mental illness are subtle, and current technologies are unable to easily capture them. Serious mental illnesses are, at their core, brain disorders with significant psychological and social components . Having a family history of mental illness and trauma are primary risk factors for major mental disorders. These strong environmental influences make it challenging to precisely separate the influences that biological factors and psychosocial considerations have on mental illnesses.

In addition, researchers conceptualize psychiatric disorders not as discrete illnesses but behavioral syndromes : a constellation of signs and symptoms that overlap each other. For example, anxiety and mood disorders have overlapping signs and symptoms, and patients often meet criteria concurrently for both sets of disorders. The same is true of schizophrenia and bipolar disorder with psychosis .

Characterizing each of these disorders as discrete conditions in the DSM is an oversimplification because they cluster together due to shared genetic and environmental factors. Further, conditions such as major depressive disorder and schizophrenia likely have several subgroups that superficially resemble each other but develop through different mechanisms and pathways. Finding a single biomarker that reflects multiple processes at the same time is unrealistic.

Syndromes have long existed in medicine. Diseases such as tuberculosis , cancer and diabetes were recognized as clusters of symptoms and signs before advances in science and technology could pinpoint the biological mechanisms that cause each disease.

But researchers haven’t reached that juncture with mental illnesses. Nobel Prize-winning psychiatrist and neurobiologist Eric Kandel famously wrote that “the last frontier of the biological sciences … is to understand the biological basis of consciousness and the mental processes by which we perceive, act, learn and remember.” He believed that solving this “ultimate challenge” requires merging cell biology with psychology to explain human behavior and consciousness in purely biological terms.

Although research is ongoing, there have been meaningful advances in the neurobiology of mental health since the publication of the fifth version of the DSM. I believe three advances seem particularly promising.

The first are biomarkers for Alzheimer’s disease. Until recently, diagnosing Alzheimer’s required a medical history and exam as well as postmortem evidence of two abnormal proteins associated with the disease called amyloid and tau . In March 2025, the Food and Drug Administration approved a blood test to detect specific forms of these proteins and help confirm a diagnosis of Alzheimer’s. This is the first instance of a biomarker for a disorder that affects both the brain and behavior.

The second are immune factors. The immune system has been implicated in several medical conditions , including mood disorders such as depression. For example, C-reactive protein is a molecule that the liver makes in response to injury and infection. Approximately 30% of patients with depression have high CRP levels , suggesting that it may serve as a biomarker to identify a subtype of patients who may respond better to certain types of treatment than those with lower levels of CRP.

The third are genetic risk factors. Certain genes are associated with an increased risk of developing a mental disorder. These risk genes are different from disease genes , which directly cause a disorder. Researchers have linked multiple risk genes to several mental disorders, and the effect each genetic variant has on developing a mental disorder is cumulative. Bundling these individual genetic variants into what’s called a polygenic risk score could offer a more comprehensive estimate of disease risk.
While genetic biomarkers are not ready for use in the clinic, integrating genetic and psychosocial risk factors can help psychiatry transition into the era of precision medicine .

In 2013, psychiatrist Henry Nasrallah conducted an online survey of colleagues visiting the webpage of the journal Current Psychiatry, of which he was editor-in-chief. He wrote that 65% of respondents predicted the DSM-6 will include laboratory tests to diagnose psychiatric disorders and that he believed they might be right.
Thirteen years later, researchers are finally working to introduce biology to the DSM, one finding at a time.
The DSM isn’t perfect, but it offers a common language and conceptual framework for mental health clinicians to help support patients and their families over the long haul of mental illness.

While science reveals the inconvenient truth about how complex mental disorders are, I believe incorporating neuroscience into the DSM as the research advances will provide clinicians a more scientific and broader perspective on mental health. One day, patients may be able to walk into the clinic with results from genetic tests, brain scans and blood work that their health team can use to provide more precise diagnoses and personalized treatment.
That’s the dream I have for the future of psychiatry.
Anand Kumar served on the American Psychiatric Association's DSM strategic committee and the biomarkers and biological factors subcommittee.

articles.title: Crocodiles as prison guards: Israeli moat plan dehumanizes Palestinian prisoners
articles.author:
<name>Irus Braverman, SUNY Distinguished & Dr. Teresa A. Miller Professor of Law, Adjunct Professor of Geography, and Research Professor at the Department of Environment & Sustainability, University at Buffalo</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/irus-braverman-2582282"/>
paras: When Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir proposed surrounding a prison holding Palestinian security detainees with Nile crocodiles, many people dismissed the idea as political theater .

After all, the image of crocodiles patrolling a prison moat seemed so outlandish that it was easy to treat as a publicity stunt. Similar claims were also directed at Donald Trump’s now-shuttered Alligator Alcatraz in Florida, which appeared to serve as inspiration for the new Israeli crocodile project.

Yet despite a temporary injunction by an Israeli court preventing the transfer of crocodiles to the proposed site at Ketziot prison, Ben-Gvir and others in the Israeli government are forging ahead. On Aug. 5, 2026, just three days after the Jerusalem District Court issued the injunction, Ben-Gvir and Environmental Protection Minister Idit Silman visited the site , posing on a bridge overlooking a partially constructed moat and posting defiant messages on social media.

Regardless of whether Ben-Gvir’s crocodile prison is ever constructed, the very existence of this plan is revealing. As someone who studies the intersection of settler colonialism and environmental governance , I believe it highlights a longer history in which animals have been weaponized to advance settler colonial projects of dispossession, territorial control and dehumanization.

Nile crocodiles were thriving in parts of what are now Israel and the Palestinian territories until the late 19th century. But habitat destruction and the drainage of wetlands in the area during the late Ottoman and British mandate periods led to their eradication from the region by the early 20th century, a process that unfolded in tandem with the dispossession of local marsh-dwelling communities from this area.

Decades later, crocodiles reappeared in the region in a radically different role – not as wild animals, but as commodities. They were brought back through crocodile farms, which marketed the animals as tourist attractions and sought to profit from their skins for the luxury leather trade.
While crocodiles have been classified as “protected wildlife” under Israeli law since the 1950s, a 1990 amendment carved out an exception by introducing the category of “cultivated wildlife.”

Subsequently, in the 1990s and 2000s, crocodile farms emerged across Israel and the Palestinian territories. One of the most prominent farms was at Hamat Gader, a tourist site near the Jordanian border, where visitors watched handlers wrestle crocodiles, force open their jaws and flip them onto their backs. These spectacles drew criticism from animal welfare advocates, who sued the farm. Their challenge became the first major test of Israel’s newly enacted 1994 animal welfare law .

The resulting decision — Let the Animals Live v. Hamat Gader — is widely regarded as a landmark ruling on animal welfare in Israeli law. The court concluded that the suffering inflicted on the crocodiles could not be justified by the entertainment provided to visitors, recognizing animals as subjects of legal concern rather than mere property.

In 2007, the Israeli government moved to formally declare three species – American alligators, ostriches and Nile crocodiles – as falling under the “cultivated wildlife” category created nearly two decades earlier by the amendment to the Israeli environmental law. This special legal category provided official permits for the animals’ commercial breeding, while they remained subject to state supervision.

Meanwhile, however, crocodiles escaping from the farms triggered public safety concerns. By the early 2010s, officials concluded that the breeding experiment had failed and revoked the “cultivated wildlife” designation.
But then there was another problem: What to do with hundreds of captive crocodiles that could neither be released nor easily relocated?

The dilemma became particularly visible in 2025, when Israeli authorities killed 262 crocodiles at a breeding facility in the Jordan Valley. The officials argued that the facility was negligent in caring for the animals and that the crocodiles therefore posed a public safety risk that justified the violent measures.

In 2026, acting on Ben-Gvir’s request, environmental minister Silman revived the dormant category of “cultivated wildlife” to allow state agencies to keep crocodiles for what she classified as “security purposes.”
This decision has encountered widespread opposition from Israeli nature conservation experts and legal advisers, including the environment minister’s own legal adviser .

In addition to crocodile welfare issues, critics have pointed out that crocodiles are poorly suited for prison security: They spend long periods inactive, especially in cooler weather, and modern prisons already possess far more effective technologies for surveillance and confinement.
In an urgent appeal to Silman on Aug. 16 , 36 of Israel’s top ecologists and conservation experts warned about the dire consequences of such a move to both the crocodiles and the public at large.
“The question of who those prisoners are is not relevant,” they wrote in the appeal. “The question is who we are, what we want to be, and how we want to be seen by ourselves and by the world.”

Despite the broad opposition, Ben-Gvir has remained resolute, previously declaring : “Whoever murdered, massacred and raped, and behaved like an animal, deserves to be guarded by an animal, exactly like them.”

His comments reveal the crux of the matter. Crocodiles are not deployed here because they are efficient security tools. Rather, their appeal lies in what they symbolize: ancient, armored and predatory, crocodiles evoke fears that prison walls, cameras and sensors do not.

Ben-Gvir and Silman’s visit to the prison on Aug. 5 underscored this message. Speaking to the cameras, Silman proclaimed that the crocodiles’ welfare outside would surely be much better than that of the Palestinian prisoners inside .

The comparison drawn here between humans and nonhumans is telling. It fits a form of dehumanization that I refer to as “ zoometrics .” When a human is compared to an unliked animal – as Palestinians regularly have been – then the perceived value of the human diminishes even lower than of that animal. Studies across diverse geopolitical contexts , including my own work , have shown that such comparisons often precede – and can thus predict – acts of extreme violence.

The temporary injunction against transferring the crocodiles to the prison remains in effect while the case proceeds through the court system. Meanwhile, Ben-Gvir condemned the injunction as pro-terrorist and has been continuing construction at full speed . The Israeli government has already allocated around US$7 million for the project and hired an expert architect to design the structures , which include shade for the crocodiles.

The crocodile’s journey under Israeli law – from protected wildlife to commercial commodity and, finally, potential security asset – reveals that legal classifications do not only regulate animals; they also determine their prospects for life or death .
More broadly, the crocodile prison proposal demonstrates how settler colonial agendas enlist and weaponize not only humans but also animals and environments.

This dynamic is not unique to crocodiles. Israel has been training and deploying its own dogs for military combat while simultaneously rescuing dogs the Gaza Strip in humanitarian missions and finding them new Israeli homes. Likewise, settler-owned sheep , donkeys, goats and cows have been deployed by Israeli shepherds for territorial takeover, whereas the same animals , when owned by Palestinian pastoralists, have been subjected to violent attacks .
The crocodile is merely the latest example of Israel’s ongoing weaponization of nonhuman life.

articles.title: Why French officials placed a Muslim war memorial in the intellectual heart of Paris in the 20th century
articles.author:
<name>Shannon Fogg, Professor of History, Missouri University of Science and Technology</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/shannon-fogg-2593133"/>
paras: The Paris Grand Mosque, an iconic cultural landmark located in the heart of the city, is celebrating its centenary . Built as a war memorial to honor Muslim soldiers killed during World War I, it was the first permanent mosque in the French capital and remains its only mosque built with a minaret and a dome. The story behind its construction reflects the politics of colonialism in interwar Paris.

While estimates vary, scholars generally agree that more than 500,000 men from the French empire , including North African, West African and Southeast Asian countries , fought for France between 1914 and 1918. These troops were deployed in critical areas and suffered high casualty rates . Muslims represented approximately 70% of the 100,000 colonial soldiers killed in battle. During and after the war, France sought ways to recognize the sacrifices of its Muslim subjects.

As a professor of French history , I regularly offer classes on war and society in 20th-century Europe. I teach my students how to “read” the war memorials that appeared across the world in the 1920s and ’30s to mourn the dead. Their symbolic messages often tell us more about politics and society than they reveal about the soldiers killed in battle. The Paris Grand Mosque is no exception.

During the war, a former colonial agronomy school on the outskirts of Paris was converted to a temporary hospital for soldiers from the empire. A wooden mosque , known as the Nogent Mosque, was added to the site in 1916 to serve the large number of Muslim patients at the hospital.

The French minister of foreign affairs described the mosque as a way to recognize the sacrifices made by Muslim soldiers, but it was not meant to be permanent. It closed in 1919 after colonial soldiers returned home and was demolished in the 1920s. By then, construction of the Grand Mosque had begun with support from the French government and African colonial administrations.

On paper, a North African religious association would be responsible for building and managing the Grand Mosque as well as an attached Muslim educational institute. The Society of Habous and Sacred Lands of Islam was founded in 1917 to facilitate North African Muslims’ annual pilgrimage to Mecca and Medina during the war. By 1920, the private society headed the state-supported project of creating a new monument in Paris.

French politicians supported this arrangement for several reasons. First, it created legitimacy for the mosque . Supporters emphasized that it was designed for and by Muslims with little government intervention. Second, it allowed officials to avoid violating the law separating church and state.

The law of Dec. 9, 1905 , recognized freedom of religion, but it prohibited using public funds to support religious entities. Instead, French politicians provided 500,000 francs to the Society of Habous for construction costs to protect the appearance of religious neutrality.

With partial funding in place, the Society of Habous needed a building site. Original proposals placed the Grand Mosque near Les Invalides , a set of buildings that serve as a shrine to France’s military heroes. But rather than building it near the existing complex, it was constructed on vacant land in the Latin Quarter, the intellectual heart of the city.

This new location was chosen for its availability, but it provided supporters with additional talking points. French politicians claimed that the prime location in central Paris reflected France’s deep respect for Islam . Additionally, its proximity to the Sorbonne , the country’s oldest and most prestigious university, further underlined the educational and secular nature of the endeavor.

The locale also reflected French colonial thinking. A book published after the mosque’s inauguration by a French civil servant named René Weiss argued that Muslims visiting Paris would benefit from “ the benevolent virtues of French civilization ” through its location in the neighborhood “from which French thought shines.” In other words, French culture, he hoped, would positively influence Islam.

Built between 1922 and 1926, the Grand Mosque housed a prayer room, a library, a hammam – or public bath – a hostel and a restaurant. It was both a religious and secular site that was open to Muslims, the Parisian public and tourists. As author and journalist Moustafa Bayoumi argues, it put Islam on display. But the recognition of Muslim soldiers’ sacrifices was less visible.

Government officials regularly described the Grand Mosque as a war memorial. In 1921, Albert Sarraut, the minister of colonies , called the mosque a symbol of “Franco-Muslim fraternity … sealed on the battlefields.” At the groundbreaking ceremony in 1922, Paris municipal councilor Paul Fleurot said the new Muslim institute “will exist as a commemorative monument raised to the memory of those Muslim soldiers who died for France.”

After the war, monuments to war dead appeared across France. More than 35,000 war monuments reinforced the secular values of the French Third Republic in public spaces by focusing on equality of sacrifice and drawing on republican symbols. These monuments did not include religious symbols and were built outside of cemeteries and churches. Hundreds of similar monuments were built in colonial Algeria during the interwar period.

Historian Jan C. Jansen argues that the colonial monuments were meant to symbolize the continued unity between France and her empire after the war through similar forms of commemoration. But he also explains how the monuments deliberately marked the differences between French citizens and colonial subjects: Monuments erected in Algeria, for example, featured statues of French soldiers and listed the names of European soldiers separately from indigenous soldiers.

The building of a North African mosque in the French capital was also a way to recognize Muslim soldiers, but this message is often hidden to visitors. The Paris history marker located outside the entrance does not mention World War I. There is no list of soldiers’ names on display , a common postwar commemorative practice.
It was not until 2014 that French President François Hollande dedicated two wall plaques inside the Grand Mosque recognizing the Muslim soldiers who fought for France in each of the world wars.
One hundred years after its inauguration, the Grand Mosque of Paris still tells a story of politics and society – as a Muslim war memorial built in the context of a secular, colonial state.

articles.title: Slog AM: Dolly Parton Died, Tim Curry Died, I’m Too Sad to Do the Real News
articles.author: Megan Seling
paras: Yesterday, Dolly Parton died. I can’t think of another person who was so widely beloved. It felt like a global day of mourning as thousands of tributes poured in from every direction. I loved her, too. So yes, we’ll do the news this morning, but let’s also remember just a few of the ways in which Dolly Parton was an anomaly, an angel, a once-in-a-lifetime talent , and a once-in-a-lifetime human being . She maneuvered sexism in the music and film industry with humor and grace, and while she never officially endorsed any political candidates or claimed a party, she talked with her money and actions. She encouraged people to be kind, to lead with love . May we all go forth with a little bit more kindness in the coming days, for Dolly.

And just as we were about to hit publish on this post, we learned Rocky Horror Picture Show and Monty Python star and comedy legend Tim Curry died . Dolly would probably make some joke about how “Isn’t it just like a man to try to steal her spotlight, even in death?” And he would laugh and laugh because he was also kind and funny, and I hate today; I’m going back to bed.

Starbucks Workers United is calling for a nationwide boycott . On the website , union organizers write, “What we’re fighting for is simple: a minimum $17 per hour wage, enough hours to live on, better staffing in our stores, and basic workplace protections.” They also point out, “Starbucks has violated U.S. labor law more than any other company in modern history.” In December, Starbucks had to pay $35 million to more than 15,000 workers “to settle claims it violated labor law.”

💖 Dolly Parton was pro-worker! Though her song “9 to 5” was written for the movie of the same name, both she and filmmakers Colin Higgins and Patricia Resnick were also inspired by the National Association of Working Women’s organization, 9to5 , which was founded in 1973 and fought for equal rights and fair pay. The song—and the scene in which Parton and costars Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin get stoned and fantasize about killing their sexist boss—left a hell of a legacy as women continue to fight for equality. In 2018, Alice Bag teamed up with Kathleen Hanna and Allison Wolfe to recreate scenes from the movie for the music video for Bag’s song, “77.”

Will Seattle teachers strike? Today, members of the Seattle Education Association (SEA) are holding a general meeting where they will either ratify a tentative contract or authorize a strike. Collective bargaining began in June, and in a recent update , SEA Vice President Davina Diaz said two of the important issues they’re negotiating are “pressurization and wages.” She continued:

“When we say pressurization, we mean relief from the increases in caseload, class size, and workload that take our time and focus away from students and lead to burnout. … Budgets are moral documents that show who matters, and who doesn’t. The spending on highly-paid administrators paints a clear picture of priorities that don’t align with what our students need.”

💖 You know who looooved educators? Dolly Fuckin’ Parton! In 2022, the National Education Association awarded Dolly Parton with their highest honor, the Friend of Education Award . Y’all already know about the Imagination Library, which has sent hundreds of millions of free books to children all over the world for years. What not everyone remembers, though, is that in the early days of the Dollywood Foundation, founded in 1988, Parton promised seventh- and eighth-grade students in Sevier County, Tennessee, where she grew up, that she would personally pay them $500 if they graduated from high school. At the time, the dropout rate was about 30 percent. It plummeted to 6 percent after Parton intervened. In 2000, she introduced the Dolly Parton Scholarship, giving $15,000 to five high school Sevier County seniors. You hear that, Seattle Public Schools? In the name of Dolly, I implore you to PAY! THE! TEACHERS!

Speaking of paying up, Meta has agreed “to pay up to $17.1 billion in penalties and make major changes to its products over claims it endangered children with addictive social media platforms,” says the New York Times .

articles.title: Op-Ed: Land Value Capture Could Fund Ballard Light Rail
articles.author: Aaron Schechter
paras: Sound Transit is facing a significant budget issue, with a roughly 10-billion-dollar budget gap in its planned light rail expansions, even after cuts and delays announced in May . Ballard Link faces the largest expected budget shortfall, but one revenue tool could help get the project back on track: a value capture strategy using tax-increment financing (TIF).

Sound Transit 3 (ST3), approved by voters in 2016, is meant to deliver the West Seattle Link Extension, the Ballard Link Extension, the 4 Line light rail from Issaquah to South Kirkland, and more. The budget rebalancing in May required that Sound Transit make a lot of significant concessions, most notably terminating the Ballard line at Seattle Center, tabling three stations indefinitely, including one of the project’s highest projected ridership stations : Ballard.

Earlier this month, Sound Transit revealed that 2042 was its best case scenario opening date for Ballard Link, while the three deferred stations would slip to around 2060 without inventions to cut costs and find new revenue.

Value capture taxes function by making a very powerful inference. When rapid transit is built, land around the stations becomes more valuable , often dramatically more so. In a normal transit-building scenario, the additional tax collected from the land value increase goes to the same services that they typically would have. More money for the City and County budget, more money for the school district, and more…, all made possible by the train. Increased property value and tax revenue that transit creates is clearly a good thing for local governments, and is yet another reason that building rapid transit is an amazing decision.

A few different types of value capture taxes exist, but the main one I’m focusing on is called tax increment financing, often referred to as TIF. Tax increment financing operates by taking out a large loan, ‘freezing’ the property values at a certain number and point in time, and then allocating any additional tax gained from an increase in property value to pay back the loan that funded the project.

The Ballard Link Extension is in serious jeopardy. If the extension all the way to 15th and Market Street doesn’t happen, or is delayed until the 2060s as feared, then there will be billions of dollars in property tax income (among many other significant benefits) that will vanish into thin air. This would be a truly historic fumble. Instead, Sound Transit can work with the city of Seattle to capture future property value increase!
That increased value will literally not exist if the project doesn’t happen. The increased value will exist if the project does happen.

Please note that for this article, I am speaking exclusively about land value, not the improved value upon the land. Read my land value tax article for more about that distinction. Also note that improvement value around the rapid transit stations, unaffected by a value capture tax, typically increases substantially. This creates tax revenue for the city that usually well outpaces the value lost to the financing vehicle.
See this graph below to visualize the different aspects of a TIF district

The image above is illustrative and is meant to communicate the general idea of a TIF, and not to calculate exact numbers. The 30 year TIF term is not set in stone and is often adjusted based on the amount of money the TIF zone brings in. The $1.077 billion in 2018 and $1.926 billion in 2027 are both real data points representing the land value within 2,000 feet of 15th and Market. All other data seen are projected.

Value capture taxes are not novel in our region. We can look towards a recent example of a local improvement district (LID) funding a prominent Seattle victory: Waterfront Park. Completed in 2025, Waterfront Park is the culmination of the project started long ago with the digging of the SR 99 tunnel and the teardown of the Alaskan Way Viaduct. This has become an amazing part of our city and was recently on display during the World Cup . Without taxing the district directly benefitting the most , the Waterfront Park project may not have been possible, and the benefitting properties would not have found the same increase in value to their land.

LIDs are similar to TIFs, but directly tax property owners in the region rather than ‘capturing’ a portion of the increased tax revenue like a TIF does. Read about Seattle’s Waterfront Park LID here , and LIDs in general here .

A second example comes from our neighbors on the other side of the 2 Line: Bellevue. In an effort to fund the Grand Connection , five different local government authorities, including Sound Transit, approved the TIF plan for this project. King County Councilmember Claudia Balducci said she hopes this sets a precedent for other parts of King County to use this funding mechanism. The Grand Connection, if built, will provide a lot of value to the surrounding areas. Read all about this project in The Urbanist .

The area around 15th and Market in Ballard is already valuable land, but will become much more so if and when the light rail is completed. The area today features a huge amount of car activity and space dedicated to the personal automobile, including large parking lots at Walgreens and Safeway, a gas station, and the gigantic streets themselves. A completed light rail line would allow that area to enjoy far more economic activity.

For this data analysis and visualization, I took data from the King County Assessor, who publishes an extensive data download page with property tax information going back over 15 years. For this analysis I used the most up to date data, 2027, to compare with data from 2018. Check out this chart showing the mean increase in land value in the 2000 feet around various light rail stations and non light rail stations. Due to their differences in land use patterns I chose to exclude downtown and SoDo light rail stations from this analysis. Downtown sports high density, whereas the SoDo stations are surrounded by lots of industrial land. These areas are rather different from the nine station areas studied, which primarily have medium density and mixed land uses, making them relatively comparable.

Below is a bar graph showing the amount that land around various points has increased in value over the past nine years. Note the clear increase around the light rail stations. Correlation or causation?

Now let’s visualize some of those numbers. First, take a look at this map of the entire city, aggregated into hexagons, showing the median increase from 2018 to present in that hexagon. You can almost see the path of the light rail. The northern stations (University District, Roosevelt, and Northgate) have only been open since 2021, but the stations in South Seattle all have had time to reap the benefits of the train access and are significantly more valuable than they were in 2018.
Now take a look at the map below, showing individual parcels in the 2,000 foot radius around their respective center points.

Note that in the nine years between the 2018 and 2027 assessments, some parcels have been divided and new ones created in their place. Consequently, a direct 1 to 1 comparison is not possible in those instances. For this reason, as well as certain public property not being evaluated in the same way (such as public universities and parks), not all parcels will show in these maps. This applies, albeit less frequently, to the aggregated hexagon maps.

Additionally, you may have noticed some sections where there are groups of parcels that all uniformly increased in value, such as in the eastern portion of the Ballard circle. This is usually caused by upzoning which makes the land instantly more valuable, as more types/density can be added to those lots.

The land in a 2,000-foot radius around Ballard Station (15th and Market) is currently worth close to $2 billion ($1,926,924,400 to be exact). Seattle’s property tax rate is just shy of 1% (often denoted as $10 per $1000 in value), meaning that the land around Ballard Station brings in about $19 million.

Note that the 2,000 foot radius chosen for this study is an arbitrary size within the typical range and not the letter of the law. TIF areas have no uniform radius and are often not circles at all. If this were to be implemented, the powers that be would decide which properties are within the area most affected by the new station and include them in the TIF district.

If a TIF district were to be made for those properties within a 2,000-foot radius, and land value grows 250% in nine years, as could be reasonably expected based on value growth surrounding light rail stations since 2017 (see initial bar graph), we can translate that to 10% per year. If that 10% per year is ‘captured’ and all the growth goes to funding ST3, a TIF district would yield $114 million in its first decade, $718 million in its first 20 years and a generous $2.59 billion in a 30-year period. $2.59 billion is a significant portion of the $7 billion to $9 billion funding gap facing the Ballard Link Extension.

This $2.59 billion over 30 years at 10% value growth per year may not be realistic. There are a huge amount of variables at play here, such as the radius of the financing zone, the percentage of the value increase allocated to Sound Transit, the increase in land value and more. Also keep in mind that this was calculated for just one station, but could be applied to many more stations, such as Interbay, Smith Cove, the extremely high land value Denny Station, and even stations on the West Seattle and 4 Line stations at Eastgate and Central Issaquah.

A value capture tax could find a lot of money for transit that otherwise would not exist. Ballard Station will provide staggering positive externalities to the community, and if the agency executing the project can capture just some of them, maybe the train will actually see the light at the end of the tunnel.
Thanks for reading. You can check out my code for the project here , and please don’t hesitate to reach out with your thoughts at aaron.m.schechter@gmail.com.

articles.title: Seattle’s AI weed wars: One startup maps them, another zaps them
articles.author: John Cook
paras: The next big test for AI isn’t happening in a data center. It’s happening in the dirt.
Two Seattle-area startups are betting that AI can transform how farmers find and eliminate unwanted plants — one by mapping every weed, the other by zapping them with lasers.

Issaquah, Wash.-based TerraClear is commercializing a new system that uses ultra-high-resolution imagery and machine learning to map individual weeds across entire fields of corn and soybeans, then turns those detections into digital prescriptions that can be sent directly to precision sprayers.
The new Weed Maps technology from TerraClear — best known for its robotic rock picking technology — can identify weeds as small as a quarter of an inch, the company said in a press release today .
Meanwhile, Seattle-based Carbon Robotics is taking a different approach: Its autonomous LaserWeeder uses computer vision to identify weeds and then blasts them with lasers.

Now, the AI powering these systems is getting smarter, too — moving beyond simple weed detection toward models that can recognize and understand plants across different crops, fields and growing conditions.

TerraClear’s new Weed Maps, announced Tuesday, captures imagery at 1.5-millimeter resolution and identifies weeds as small as the eraser on a pencil. Rather than sampling portions of a field, the company says it collects images of every acre and produces a geo-referenced map that can be uploaded to section or nozzle-controlled sprayers used by farmers.
The goal is precision at a level that would be difficult for a human to achieve, allowing a farmer to know where the individual weeds are.
TerraClear says the maps can be delivered the next day, giving growers a chance to act while weeds are still small and easier to control.

Devin Lammers, the chief executive of TerraClear, tells GeekWire that its approach “sidesteps the capital problem entirely.” In other words, farmers need not buy a new piece of expensive equipment, instead using software to turn existing sprayers into precision instruments by telling them exactly where to spray.
He called Carbon Robotics laser-weeding system “impressive technology,” noting that it works well for specialty crops and organics.
But bigger farms producing commodity crops like corn and soybeans — the market TerraClear is going after — need a different approach, he said.

“Modern grain and oilseed sprayers already have individual nozzle control and RTK positioning — the actuation hardware is sitting in the shed,” Lammers said via email. “We just hand the sprayer a shapefile of individual weed locations and it turns the nozzle on only where a weed actually is.”
Given that large corn and soybean growers farm more acres at a lower revenue per acre, Lammers said it’s a “very different P&L” where expensive new equipment needs to pencil out.
With TerraClear’s new system, Lammers added that “the farmer buys a map, not a machine.”

One of the benefits of both approaches is chemical use reduction in the field, a hot topic in political circles with President Trump earlier this year committing $1 billion to modernize farming and reduce chemicals in agriculture. That federal investment could help spark new innovations, like the ones TerraClear and Carbon Robotics are developing.

Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the U.S. secretary of health and human services, earlier this year touted Carbon Robotics’s machines on an episode of The Joe Rogan Experience as a possible solution in cutting pesticide use.
In the case of TerraClear, Lammers said the precision mapping technology alone could cut pesticide and herbicide use by up to 80% with no loss of efficacy.
Both startups are part of a broader Pacific Northwest ag-tech ecosystem that has been applying AI and robotics to agriculture, building on the regions farming and tech roots.

TerraClear founder Brent Frei represents that unique farming and tech DNA. He grew up on a family farm in Grangeville, Idaho, before studying at Dartmouth and then moving to the Seattle area where he co-founded Onyx Software and Smartsheet.

Founded in 2017, TerraClear originally attacked a much less glamorous agricultural problem: identifying and removing rocks from farmers’ fields. In 2024, the company raised $15 million, bringing its total funding to $53 million.

By February of this year, TerraClear had expanded to about 50 employees and was approaching 1,000 customers. At that time, it also launched an autonomous field robot called TerraScout , designed to collect high-resolution imagery across a field and convert that information into actionable maps for existing farm equipment.
The company says TerraScout can collect more than 4 billion image samples per acre and map more than 1,000 acres a day under favorable conditions.
In addition to TerraScout, Lammers said they are using aerial drones to ingest field-level data into its new Weed Maps product.

“That’s the part that compounds — the imagery we gather is field-level, repeated season over season, and specific to the commodity acre,” Lammers said. “Models get better, which makes the maps better, which brings more acres, which produces more data.”
Carbon Robotics is further down the road in making the machine the decision-maker, and eradicating weeds without the use of chemicals.

The Seattle startup’s LaserWeeder combines cameras, AI and high-powered lasers to identify weeds and destroy them without applying herbicides or pesticides. The company has deployed its machines on farms around the world and has built an enormous dataset in the process.

Announced in February, its so-called Large Plant Model was trained on 150 million labeled plants, which Carbon describes as the largest agricultural plant dataset of its kind. The company’s goal is to move beyond narrowly trained computer-vision systems that need to be retrained whenever a new weed or field condition appears.
With the Large Plant Model, farmers can use Carbon’s Plant Profiles feature to show the system a handful of images and customize what the machine should recognize and target.

Given the changing dynamics of a weed during various stages of its growth — and based on conditions such as soil, weather and crop varieties — Carbon wants to correctly identify the difference between a weed and a crop.

“When our robots can understand any plant in any field immediately and adapt behavior in real-time, farmers immediately get maximum value from the machines,” Carbon Robotics CEO Paul Mikesell said in a press release . “The Large Plant Model provides farmers with the most advanced AI technology to maximize the weeding quality of LaserWeeder in their unique environments.”
Founded in 2018, Carbon Robotics has raised $177 million to date and as of last year employed about 260 people at offices in Seattle and a manufacturing facility in Richland, Wash.
TerraClear and Carbon Robotics are attacking one of agriculture’s thorniest problems — weed management — from different directions.
TerraClear wants to allow a farmer to keep using a conventional precision sprayer, while making it dramatically more selective via its Weed Maps.
Carbon, meanwhile, is developing autonomous laser-weeding equipment itself, identifying and eliminating the individual weeds in real time without chemical spray or tractor operators.
The bigger opportunity for both companies may ultimately be neither maps nor lasers, but the underlying data they gather.

Every time a camera passes over a field, it can collect information about plants, soil, crop health and growing conditions. That’s vital information to farmers, seed producers, agriculture researchers and equipment manufacturers.

articles.title: In another multimillion land deal for a Capitol Hill grocery, Hillcrest Market has new ownership
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Another of Capitol Hill’s vital neighborhood markets has a new owner amid reminders that Capitol Hill’s relentless waves of redevelopment continue to churn.
In June , CHS reported on new ownership for Bellevue Ave’s much-loved City Market as part of a $7.5 million land deal for the property.
Now, Summit Ave E’s Hillcrest Market also has a new shopkeep.

Randhir Singh has taken over the grocery after buying the property for $3.95 million late last year, according to King County records. The litany of permits required to run a neighborhood market including licenses for cigarette, tobacco, and vapor product retailing, beer and wine sales, and lottery sales finally transferred under the new owner earlier this month.
Hillcrest, perhaps best known as the host for the original Carmelo’s Tacos , provides a mix of groceries, convenience items, and deli food typical of the neighborhood’s corner shops.
For now, it is business as usual at Hillcrest — that could, of course, change.

Singh’s transaction included the neighboring H Cleaners property where permit work is listed as “in process” with the city for a soil boring project typically part of environmental site assessment and “plume tracking” of potential contaminants from the decades of dry cleaning service done at the location. That kind of work is often part of pre-development engineering for mixed-use projects. Any redevelopment is years away.

As with City Market just down the hill, Hillcrest’s immediate daily operations remain intact even as the underlying real estate is primed for change. With plans for soil samples to be pulled from the sidewalk and major capital already deployed, the groundwork is being laid for the next changes along E Olive Way.

articles.title: A change in how CHS gathers 911 information as Seattle Fire radio encryption cuts off most scanner access
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Monday night brought the first major neighborhood emergency for CHS to cover without a vital information source we have used for years to report on 911 incidents across Capitol Hill and the Central District.
Last week, the Seattle Fire Department began encrypting most of its emergency radio channels, cutting off real-time public and scanner access to tactical and operational channels.
The rollout, powered by the digital Puget Sound Emergency Radio Network , aligns operations between SFD, the Seattle Police Department , and regional partner agencies.

While SPD began encrypting its tactical talkgroups, SWAT maneuvers, and sensitive data queries during its initial phase earlier this year, SFD finalized the regional push in mid-August. By August 31, most fire channels will be fully encrypted, silencing live tactics, Mayday transmissions, and paramedic hospital communications.

Officials announced the planned phase-in last year , saying the upgrades were necessary to “enhance the safety of community members and first responders, and to protect the public’s sensitive information from being shared to a wide audience.”
Seattle Fire cited patient medical privacy under HIPAA, responder safety during dynamic scenes, and the security of private building access codes as the primary drivers behind their policy.

To preserve baseline transparency, both Seattle Fire and SPD have said they are keeping primary dispatch broadcasts unencrypted. Newsrooms and scanner listeners will continue hearing initial call types, general locations, and dispatched units over the air, while encrypted audio remains subject to post-incident release under Washington’s Public Records Act.

While each SPD dispatch channel including the East Precinct covering Capitol Hill and the Central District continues to broadcast details about the dispatch incidents in addition to location, the remaining open Seattle Fire communications will apparently be extremely limited and focused mostly on the automated system broadcasting only an incident’s category and location along with one of the most irritating klaxon signals ever devised. Listen to the example below to get the idea.
SPD’s dispatch remains human-formed and relatively detailed — for now.

As for gathering Seattle Fire information, Monday night’s fire on E Republican provided an example of how the department says it plans to help keep the public informed as the @seattlefire account provided a series of six updates on the incident.
For smaller incidents not worthy of the larger social media feed, SFD’s Public Information Officers are available to look up incident information for journalists.

CHS used these resources and Seattle Fire updates as part of our reporting Monday night but additional details provided by readers via text messages and the CHS Facebook Group were vital. We would have missed key details without the help and the human end of SPD East Precinct radio broadcasts where we got a few important bulletins including a couple updates on the scared little Chihuahua that fled the burning building and was being watched by a group of neighbors until it could be reunited.

articles.title: Children in a Faith-Healing Sect Keep Dying. The State Lets It Happen.
articles.author: Audrey Dutton
paras: A sheriff’s deputy opens the door of an Idaho farmhouse where a newborn baby has just died. It’s almost 10 p.m., but the house is filled with adults and children seated anywhere they can find a spot: in reclining chairs, on the wood-stove hearth, on a chest of drawers. Some of the women hold babies in their laps.
“Sorry,” the deputy whispers as the door creaks.
No one greets the officer. No one speaks or even looks at anyone else, casting their eyes instead at the floor or around the room.

The deputy’s video camera records as he walks through the front room and past a bedroom door adorned with children’s artwork. Inside the bedroom, newborn Malachi’s mother sits in a recliner. His body lies in her lap, covered by a blue blanket.

As people in uniform ask Malachi’s parents about his birth, death and the two days in between, members of the family’s church — one of at least four Followers of Christ churches in Idaho — watch from folding chairs. People come and go from the bedroom; one woman cradles a sleeping toddler.
Malachi died from pneumonia and bleeding lungs, according to an autopsy.
It would have been treatable with antibiotics and newborn care in a hospital, said doctors who reviewed his death records for ProPublica.

But Malachi’s parents belong to a faith-healing sect that doesn’t believe in medical care, based on a literal interpretation of several Bible verses. The Followers of Christ sect believes that God heals the faithful and that life and death must be left to God’s divine will.

When the coroner’s deputy lifted Malachi’s body to take it away that night in October 2023, there was no wailing or sobbing from his parents. Malachi’s father stood quietly as his mother hung her head and rested it in her hand.

A pediatrician who reviewed Malachi’s death records said a baby in his condition would have been gasping for air, turning blue from lack of oxygen and breathing so hard that the outline of his rib cage was visible.
It was the first time the coroner and sheriff sent their deputies out to that house, to interview those parents and document the slow suffocation of a newborn boy.
The next time was 13 months later, when their next newborn, Liam, died from the same treatable condition that killed his brother Malachi.

In any Idaho household not steeped in faith-healing, those two deaths would be investigated as crimes. Idaho law says parents can’t endanger, injure or neglect their children or let them suffer . To do so is a crime, and if the child dies as a result, the parent could be charged with manslaughter.

But those laws do not apply to children like Malachi and Liam. Since the 1970s, Idaho’s criminal and civil laws have allowed parents who belong to Followers of Christ and the state’s other faith-healing sects to pray rather than seek medical care as their children die.

Lawmakers in Oregon, where the same religious groups exist, removed the state’s faith-healing exception to child abuse laws nearly 30 years ago, countering the overwhelming pressure former Followers say parents face from their congregations. More parents chose to get medical care for their children after the change, Oregon prosecutors and detectives said.
Idaho lawmakers have chosen a different path.

Since 2014, they have rejected repeated efforts to dial back Idaho’s faith-healing exemption, instead crafting legislation to further limit the role of anyone but a parent when it comes to children’s health and safety. The state has codified “parental rights,” banned vaccine requirements in schools and childcare centers, and made parental consent a prerequisite for medical care of minors. Legislators also have tried to narrow the definition of “medical neglect” for all families to only the most life-threatening situations, but those attempts have failed.

Local and national media outlets have reported on deaths among Followers of Christ families in Idaho. ProPublica went further, enlisting the help of experts to determine which of those deaths could have been prevented.
ProPublica gathered death records from coroners and police in five Idaho counties and shared them with more than a dozen pediatricians and birthing specialists.
At least 15 babies and children from the faith-healing sect died between 2015 and 2025 from illnesses that doctors could have successfully treated, the experts concluded.

The estimate of preventable deaths is almost certainly an undercount. The experts could not evaluate six more deaths because coroner records were incomplete or unavailable. In another four cases, they couldn’t say with confidence whether medical care would have changed the outcome.
Separately, the experts identified numerous preventable losses of babies who died during birth or in utero very close to their due dates, cases that coroners labeled as stillbirths.

For some families like Liam and Malachi’s, the death of a child wasn’t a one-time tragedy: Records show at least five sets of parents have lost multiple children, a phenomenon that has not previously been reported.

None of the parents responded to letters or text messages from ProPublica, and one declined to comment during a brief phone call. (ProPublica is choosing not to identify them or use the children’s full names out of respect for their privacy.)
But Nathan Kangas, a patriarch in the sect’s Caldwell, Idaho, church, defended faith healing and its legal protection during an interview with ProPublica.

Children and babies can’t make their own decision to rely on faith healing. Kangas said their parents must keep them away from the doctor to set an example, so the young ones won’t be cursed later in life by turning to medicine.
Kangas lost his own wife and their last child during labor 23 years ago. Three of his 65 grandchildren also have died.

Asked why God would not want children to live full and healthy lives, Kangas said he had no answer but quoted a verse from the Book of Psalms: “Precious in the eyes of the Lord are the death of His saints.” The Followers believe that life on Earth is “a preparing ground,” Kangas said. He pointed to the Book of James, which tells people to “be afflicted and mourn and weep” and “let your laughter be turned to mourning.”
“It isn’t necessarily that we’re supposed to have a joyous life here,” Kangas said. “It’s actually quite the opposite.”
Some outsiders take a very different view.

Canyon County Sheriff Kieran Donahue, one of the most vocal opponents of Idaho’s faith-healing laws, has sent deputies to follow up on the deaths of at least 10 Followers’ children and infants since he took office in 2013.
“This is needless,” Donahue said. “This shouldn’t be happening.”
David Peterman, a retired Idaho pediatrician, reviewed the deaths of 18 infants and children at ProPublica’s request.

Peterman saw patients for 40 years and did his residency at a center that offered special training in child abuse and neglect. He said the vast majority of the deaths he reviewed for ProPublica “are the result of neglect and unequivocally preventable.” (He couldn’t tell whether a few deaths were preventable, and he surmised that one infant had a fatal, untreatable chromosomal defect.) He said it is “beyond comprehension” that the Idaho Legislature has refused to change the law.
“How is this tolerable?” he said. “I don’t understand how there could be an exception in Idaho law that allows for these children to die.”

Maicy was 16 years old but the size of a third grader: 62 pounds and just shy of 4 feet tall. She had suffered from a constellation of ailments: stomach irritation, severe anemia, erratic menstrual periods, a blocked artery, thickened aorta and thinning hair. An autopsy after she died on New Year’s Day 2019 traced it all back to a benign, treatable pituitary tumor.

Doctors who reviewed her death records said her stunted growth would have been obvious earlier in childhood, when her tumor could have been diagnosed and treated. Instead, it sent her body into a hormonal tailspin that destroyed her organs. She died in bed, lying on a towel and absorbent pad, wearing a diaper under her sweatpants and a T-shirt that read “LOVE.”

Some of the children who died preventable deaths over a decade were sick for hours or days; others endured months or — in Maicy’s case — years of disease. Most died in their parents’ arms. Many would have experienced pain and distress from their untreated conditions, the healthcare professionals consulted by ProPublica said.

“I don’t know how to come to terms with that,” said Beth Hartman, an Idaho midwife and former chair of the state’s midwifery licensing board. “Because when you see respiratory distress, and when you have seen a person pass, it’s not pretty. They don’t just close their eyes.”

In America at large, the risk that a child will die is highest during the first year of life. The vast majority of Followers’ children who died were infants. But nationally, fatalities in this age group tend to follow premature birth or profound congenital disorders. The deaths among Followers’ infants came from ailments that rarely take children’s lives.

articles.title: Where to Eat By the Water in Seattle
articles.author: EverOut Staff
paras: One of the main perks of living in a city surrounded by rivers, lakes, canals, bays, and, of course, one very large Sound is that waterfront dining is usually within reach. And while smoked salmon and clam chowder will always be our staples, Seattle has just about every version of the “on the water” experience you could ask for: fish and chips on Elliott Bay, tacos after a long paddle around Portage Bay, oysters overlooking the very boats that hauled them in, and even brunch with an uninterrupted view of our iconic skyline. Sure, good food tastes good just about anywhere. But add some salty air, crashing waves, ferry boat horn blasts, and the occasional (socially distanced) hungry seagull? Now that’s Seattle.

Agua Verde Cafe There are plenty of Seattle restaurants near the water, but very few that invite you to show up for a meal via kayak. That’s the appeal of Agua Verde Cafe, the beloved Portage Bay institution where breakfast burritos, frozen mango margaritas, and house-made tacos are all best enjoyed with a front-row seat to the lake. The menu has many standouts, from rockfish tacos with mango salsa to inventive veg fillings like yams and cauliflower, and there’s hardly a bad drink in the house. And if you visit during the sunny months (May–September), the seasonal Marina Cantina has fiesta vibes with an outdoor bar and regular events. If admiring the view proves to not be enough of an experience (or if the tequila courage reaches a precipice), the adjacent Agua Verde Paddle Club rents kayaks and paddleboards for some low-effort waterborne fun. LANGSTON THOMAS Northeast Seattle

articles.title: Flagging Indicator
articles.author: Dan Savage
paras: Bi female here . I’ve been seeing an ENM M/F couple for almost four months. The F was an acquaintance of mine for about two years. We are all close in age (late thirties, early forties). This is my first ethically non-monogamous relationship.

Here are the pros: they are charming and attractive; the sex is great; they are affectionate with me in public and introduce me to their friends as someone they are dating; they invite me to sleepover at their place, they cook for me, and show other acts of care; they have come over to care for me when I am sick; we have many friends in common.

And here are the cons: they have said they want to keep things light; anything close to a “define the relationship” talk only happens when we are intoxicated; they started dating someone else around the same time as me, which I only found out when I arrived at their place for a scheduled visit and their other partner hadn’t left yet; they flirt with other women in front of me; their other partner — the one they started seeing at the same time they started seeing me — is in her early 20s, as are most of the other women they flirt with. I also believe there’s a worrying power dynamic in play where these younger women are concerned. This couple often flirts with these women by proposing modeling/photoshoots, and these younger women often seem starstruck. They both have significant social media followings (she’s a model, he’s a photographer), so the young women often seem starstruck.

Since I am new to ENM I am not sure what parts of these stresses are just learning curves for me, what parts I should talk to the couple about, and what parts are simply beyond my boundaries/red flags.

You’re fucking your first couple — achievement unlocked — and they enjoy your company outside the bedroom, they’re open about you being a part of their lives, and they show up for you when you need them. As pros go, FLAGS, that’s not a bad list. God knows there are too many “ENM” couples who think “we want to keep things casual” is a magical incantation that frees them from having to treat their casual sex partners like human beings with feelings and needs of their own. So, you could’ve done a lot worse where your first experience with ENM is concerned.

Now, the way you learned this couple was seeing another woman — running into her when you arrived for your shift — was far from ideal, of course, but I wouldn’t classify it as a betrayal. If you’d already had your first drunken DTR convo, FLAGS, then you knew this couple wanted to keep things casual. While they shouldn’t have allowed you to assume you were the only other woman they were seeing, FLAGS, you also shouldn’t have made that assumption. Still, given that you were new to ENM and therefore likely to be carrying monogamous assumptions and autopilot settings into this relationship (“If we’re fucking and seeing a lot of each other that must mean we’re exclusive!”), FLAGS, this couple should’ve made it clear to you that they were still seeing/dating/fucking other women.

And while it sounds this couple is giving you a lot — a lot more than some “keep it casual” couples give their secondary partners — it also sounds like you want more. I have a hunch that you’re the one initiating those drunken “define the relationship” conversations, FLAGS, in the hope of getting a different answer out of them at some point. And that’s not an entirely irrational hope, FLAGS, as the huge number of people in committed relationships who said they wanted to “keep it light” at the outset prove. (I was pretty adamant about “keeping things casual” when I met my husband three decades ago.) So, you can keep shaking that Magic 8 Ball, FLAGS, but if you don’t get the answer you want in the next eight months — or if you don’t realize before your first hookup anniversary that their brand of not-so-casual casual is exactly what you want after all — then you’ll need to chuck that Magic 8 Ball in the trash and end this relationship while you’re still feeling relatively good about it.
As for the younger women this couple pursues…

Dangling professional opportunities in front of younger women they wanna fuck is a red flag. A professional photographer and a model with significant followings on social media have power — they have clout — and if these two are leveraging that power to get women who wouldn’t wanna fuck them into their bed… yeah, that’s not great.

While the world is disinclined to give the benefit of the doubt to anyone who dangles a professional opportunity in front of someone they wanna fuck — and quite rightly so — you’re in a better position to judge what this couple is doing, FLAGS, given that they’re doing it in front of you. If a young woman is interested in fucking this couple and if that young woman knows what this couple does for a living (two big ifs) then the offer of a photoshoot — once mutual attraction has been established — could be received/perceived as a flirty, sexy, and obvious value-add. But if this couple is dangling photoshoots in front of younger women who don’t seem particularly interested in fucking them… yeah, that’s creepy and manipulative.

That said, FLAGS, if a young adult wants to fuck a photographer and his model girlfriend because she wants to advance her career… or if she wants to fuck a photographer and his model girlfriend because she’s into them… or if she wants to fuck them because she’s into them and she wants to advance her career… that’s her choice. Adults are capable of consenting to sex, and adults consent to sex for all sorts of reasons, good and bad.

Still, FLAGS, if what you’re seeing is making you uncomfortable, address it the next time you have one of those drunken heart-to-hearts: “I know you guys would never wanna fuck anyone who didn’t wanna fuck you… and there’s clearly no shortage of people who wanna fuck you… but do you guys ever worry that one of these aspiring models might fuck you for the wrong reason and wind up feeling bad about it later?”

I married my beloved college boyfriend twenty years ago. I’ll call him Alfred. I (mostly) still adore him. We can talk for hours about art, film, and politics — and it’s actually fun and productive when we disagree. We have a variegated and satisfying sex life. When you’re married to Alfred, you tag along with him on the passionate interests he takes on every few years. Some of them fade away completely, but many linger in the background, often quite pleasingly: gourmet cooking, vinyl records, Scotch whisky. To this day, years away from his all-consuming initial infatuations, I can still occasionally be presented at dinner with an expertly crafted cassoulet and a dram of old Caperdonich with The Clash raging on the hi-fi speakers. (We’ll not discuss the mountain of dirty dishes or the coffee-sloshed countertops.)

It’s his latest obsession that’s driving me insane. Alfred, you see, has been bitten by the “fibermaxxing” bug. Now, I can tolerate — and probably benefit from — joining him in consuming various chia puddings and pungent homemade fermentation projects (again, the guy can cook). I can deal with the lectures on “resistant fiber” and the benefits of something called butyrate. But increasingly, the man has become fixated on the triumphant result of his fibermaxxing exploits: his bowel movements. I’m happy to listen to him hash out the differences between mole poblano and mole negro; I have, at his behest, learned to distinguish between north and east Highland whiskies. But I do not want to hear him describe what takes place for him behind the bathroom door, Dan, and I flatly refuse to divulge my own such information, despite his pleas. This attitude drives him nuts!

Recently, out of the blue, in a state of joyous excitement, he urged me to follow him — he had something for me to see. When he led me into the bedroom, I thought he might have something fun in mind. But he led me through the bedroom and the bathroom, where he delightedly showed me the contents of the unflushed toilet. (He didn’t seem to consider how I’d receive the stench.) I screamed. I have not recovered from this. I cannot see him in a sexual way when I think about this foul incident. He is not a toddler; I am not his mommy. There is now an icy chill between us. Do I wait for this phase, too, to pass? Or is this development a sign that the romantic part of our relationship has run its course.

I was tired of Alfred’s shit before I got to the end of your letter, TOTS, and, if I’m going to be perfectly frank, I was tired of your shit by the time I got to the end of your letter, too. My advice: Tell your idiot husband you never want to see another one of his fibermaxxed turds ever again. (Did you really need my permission to do that?) As for your sex life: If you can’t see your husband in a sexual way when you think about this foul incident, TOTS, try your best not to think about this foul incident. If you can’t help yourself — if you can’t stop yourself from thinking about it — a few CBT sessions with a skilled provider might help.

P.S. Your husband’s turds might be variegated — “ varied in appearance or color; marked with patches or spots of different colors ” — but unless you’re wearing a cheetah fursuit to bed and/or you have an untreated sexually transmitted infection, TOTS, your sex life isn’t variegated.

paras: Neumos security staff won their union election: The National Labor Relations Board tallied their votes Friday and everyone who showed up voted yes. Workers at Neumos, Barboza and The Runaway, all owned by Fokus Industries, began organizing publicly this spring , with the security staff announcing a union earlier this month . Neumos Security Union organizer Ozi Goldstein emailed The Stranger the following after results were announced:

“We achieved this result because workers already saw that they can achieve improvements to working conditions through collective action with our previous all-staff organizing as Neumos Workers United. Now we are interested in going further to secure an actual contract for security staff at Neumos. As security, our top priority is always safety, whether it’s safe shows, safe jobs, safe wages, or safe staffing. The best way we can achieve this safety for staff, patrons, and artists, is through a fair contract.”

Feds rule striking Washington workers can’t claim unemployment unless they apply for jobs: Washington workers have had the right to claim unemployment benefits while on strike since a new state law came into effect on January 1. But after a ruling by the US Department of Labor, striking workers are no longer exempted from applying for jobs as part of the process to claim unemployment benefits, the Washington State Standard reports . With 16,000 Boeing workers poised to strike in October if the company doesn’t give them a fair contract, that’s fortuitous timing for the aerospace company’s managers.

According to the rule change filed Friday by Washington’s Employment Security Division, if they don’t make striking workers apply for jobs to receive unemployment benefits, “the Department may lose federal funding for administration of the unemployment insurance program.”

Seattle teachers vote whether to authorize a strike tomorrow: Their contract is up at the end of the month, and representatives of the 6,000-strong Seattle Education Association say the district still isn’t offering to pay them enough to live here, the Seattle Times reports . Considering the school year begins on September 2, that means city leaders have about a week to make a deal before school is canceled indefinitely and parents start calling politicians complaining that they have to waste valuable time with their kids that they could be spending with their bosses.

Spokane fires caused more than $1 billion in damage: That makes the Spokane Complex fires the worst the state has ever seen, the Spokesman Review reports . The tally comes from the Spokane County Assessor, who so far has counted 833 homes destroyed by the fires. The record might not stand for long. The previous most expensive fire was also recorded in Spokane County just three years ago.

In lighter news, “There’s a big dead whale in the Port of Tacoma. Here’s what we know” is a masterclass in headline writing by the Tacoma News Tribune : If this headline were written by the Seattle Times it would read something like “This popular ocean attraction was found wrong-side up at a local harbor.” Anyway, the whale might have been struck by a cargo ship in Commencement Bay, and NOAA says the corpse does not look bloated enough with gases to risk exploding, per the Tribune .

Washington Post forced to rehire columnist fired for refusing to mourn Charlie Kirk: Karen Attiah didn’t quite get the message that local book depository magnate and CIA contractor Jeff Bezos was reflagging WaPo as a right-wing newspaper to please Trump for money before she posted after Charlie Kirk’s assassination that “Refusing to tear my clothes and smear ashes on my face in performative mourning for a white man that espoused violence.” Management likely would not have fired her had she praised a slain leader of America’s white supremacist youth movement, but in any event, a private arbitrator ruled Attiah was wrongly terminated, and she’s back on the job, the New York Times reports .

Right-wing Democrats are trying the “Independent” strategy in Nebraska too, and it’s never not embarrassing: Remember a few weeks back I brought up how the right wing of the Montana Democratic Party destroyed the organization by racing Republicans to the right and was now trying to claw back a seat in Congress by running a fake Independent candidate? There’s a similar situation going on in Nebraska : The Democrat running for US Senate dropped out, and the party central committee voted not to fill the vacancy on the ballot in a push to clear the field for a totally independent, and definitely not a Democrat, candidate.

Congressional candidate salutes grandfather “who gave his life for his country,” which was Nazi Germany: Most of the time when Western politicians praise their Nazi families’ war service, they have the good decency to hide it behind a veil of anti-communism so that everyone is too distracted thinking about the Soviet menace to remember the Holocaust. But brave New York State Sen. Peter Oberacker needed no such nuance when he posted a Facebook photo of his Nazi grandfather who died fighting the United States with the caption “I debated on whether to post this picture, my Grandfather Ludwig Oberacker who gave his life for his country. I salute all who served.” Politico dug it up last week.

articles.title: US Supreme Court Sides with Trump Administration in Attack on Mail-In Voting
articles.author: Nathalie Graham
paras: Today, the US Supreme Court issued a ruling that could, in the short term, allow the implementation of President Donald Trump’s master plan to upend mail-in voting and delegitimize legitimate voting systems just in time for a midterm election where his approval rating is lower than it has ever been.

In March, Trump issued an executive order to restrict mail-in voting to only “eligible” voters—there would be a list of these adult US citizens—and would steer the totally not underfunded US Postal Service to only deliver ballots to those individuals.

Washington, alongside 22 other states plus Washington DC, sued over this order, calling it unconstitutional. The Constitution and Congress grant states the power to run their own elections. A US District Court judge in Massachusetts issued an injunction earlier this month that blocked the executive order from taking place in the plaintiff states and later issued a second order blocking it across the country.

In a 6-3 ruling along ideological lines, the conservative losers on the US Supreme Court lifted the first injunction which barred the mail-in voting restrictions from taking place in those 23 states. According to NBC News , that Court’s ruling will likely apply to the nationwide injunction as well.

“A majority of the U.S. Supreme Court does not seem to recognize the grave threat the president’s actions pose for our democracy,” reads an emailed statement from Washington State Attorney General Nick Brown. “There is nothing hypothetical about his intent to illegally suppress legitimate votes.”
The Court has not issued a ruling on the legality of the executive order, or as Brown puts it, the ruling “does not bless the substance of the president’s actions.”

Brown’s office says it is coordinating with other states on how to respond to the Court’s ruling. “We stand ready to take action to protect the integrity of our elections and prevent this clearly unconstitutional overreach from taking effect,” Brown says.

Nothing has immediately changed for Washington state voters and for our upcoming election. Today’s ruling could allow implementation of the mail-in voting restrictions, but any future legal challenges could freeze it again. Those challenges are likely. “The president’s clear intent here is to suppress legitimate votes with powers he does not have even if his intentions were good,” says Mike Faulk, a spokesperson from Brown’s office.
